prompt:
Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

The profile below describes the moral priorities of the British electorate.

TEXT_D:
Liberal Democrats Manifesto 1997 — Summary (within 500 words)

Vision and approach
- Build a fair, free and open society that balances liberty, equality and community; spread power and opportunity widely; reject timidity and short-termism.
- Back a market economy, with active, enabling government to invest in people, correct failures, protect the environment and uphold rights.
- Decentralise power to nations, regions and local communities; make government accountable and transparent. A menu with prices: where we invest, we say how we’ll pay.

Education and skills (top priority)
- Invest £2bn a year (funded by +1p on the basic rate) to make Britain a world-leading learning society.
- Universal, high‑quality early years education for all 3–4 year‑olds; cut primary classes to ≤30 within 5 years; double spending on books/equipment; fix crumbling buildings.
- Raise standards: General Teaching Council; focused Minimum Curriculum Entitlement; strong literacy drive; better discipline, inspection and transparent results.
- Partnerships: empower parents, school councils and communities; bring grant‑maintained/CTCs into a light‑touch local framework; phase out Assisted Places while encouraging state–independent collaboration.
- Lifelong learning: Individual Learning Accounts; income‑linked student repayments; oppose tuition top‑ups; a remissible 2% training levy (small firms exempt); credit‑based post‑14 system; wire schools to the internet.

Economy, jobs and enterprise
- Lock in stability: independent UK Reserve Bank; keep to the golden rule; responsible public/private investment; support entry to a single currency if Maastricht criteria are met and approved by referendum.
- Shift tax from jobs/consumption to pollution; promote saving and portable pensions.
- Get people back to work: turn long‑term unemployment benefits into “working benefits”; cut poverty traps; invest in skills and infrastructure.
- Back small firms: new finance, late‑payment interest, less red tape, fairer business rates, strong competition law and consumer power; modern utility regulation focused on consumers.

Environment, energy and transport
- Make sustainability central to policy; CO2 −30% from 1990 in 15 years; new quality‑of‑life indicators.
- Tax shift: gradual carbon tax offset by cuts to VAT/employers’ NICs; cut VED to £10 for ≤1600cc while raising fuel duty; reform company‑car tax.
- National Homes Insulation, starting with 2m lowest‑income households; minimum energy standards; boost renewables and CHP; no subsidies for nuclear; no replacement of nuclear stations at end of life.
- Invest in public transport; urban road pricing hypothecated to transit; keep London Underground public; double rail passengers and treble freight by 2010.
- Protect water, wildlife and countryside; greener planning; strong product labelling; robust animal‑welfare reforms; free vote on hunting.

Homes, safety and communities
- 3,000 more police on the beat; focus on prevention, restorative justice, and a drugs Royal Commission.
- Build more affordable homes via public–private–housing association partnerships; mortgage benefit for first‑time buyers; end rough sleeping by 2000; bring empty homes back into use; strengthen tenants’ rights.
- Rural and urban renewal: protect services, expand community enterprise, improve transport, safer streets.

NHS and care
- NHS comprehensive and free at point of need; +£540m yearly plus £200m for frontline staff; halt finance‑driven closures for 6 months; end two‑tier GP funding; cut waits to 6 months.
- Restore free eye/dental checks; freeze prescription charges; shift money from bureaucracy to care; national inspectorate and standards; stronger carers’ support and fairer long‑term care.

Clean politics and power sharing
- Bill of Rights; Freedom of Information; Ministry of Justice; curb quangos; referendums on constitutional change.
- Proportional representation for all elections; reduce MPs by a third; predominantly elected second chamber; fixed four‑year terms; party‑funding reform.
- Home Rule for Scotland and Wales; English regional assemblies where wanted; stronger local government; long‑term local income tax.

Opportunity and equality
- Break poverty traps: raise personal allowance; new 50% rate over £100k; simpler Low Income Benefit; minimum wage (regionally varied); childcare strategy; Citizens Service.
- Fairer pensions: earnings‑linked top‑up; flexible retirement 60–70; universal personal/occupational pensions with portability; protect older people’s and disabled people’s rights.
- Strengthen anti‑discrimination: Human Rights Commission; equal age of consent; repeal Section 28; tackle racism; civil rights for disabled.

Britain in the world
- Positive leadership in a reformed, enlarged EU; single currency if conditions met and approved by referendum.
- Strong defence via NATO and European cooperation; retain Trident with limits; curb WMD proliferation.
- UN reform, support an International Criminal Court; aid towards 0.7% GNP; strict arms‑export controls; ban landmines; fair trade with labour and environmental standards.

Tax contract
- No taxation without explanation; no promises without prices; cut waste first; fair tax for all.
- 1p on basic rate funds education; +£200 allowance and 50% top rate >£100k take ~500,000 out of tax; +5p on cigarettes funds free eye/dental checks; most adults pay the same or less.

TEXT_G:
The Statement of Aims set out four core points.

1) Why the Referendum Party? Because both major parties had embraced the Maastricht-amended Treaty on European Union, effecting a significant transfer of powers to European institutions. Such fundamental constitutional change—amounting to a relinquishment of sovereignty—should not proceed without the people’s consent. The Referendum Party’s purpose was to secure a full national debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe, followed by a fair referendum.

2) What question should be put to the people? Voters should be asked: “Do you want the United Kingdom to be part of a federal Europe or do you want the United Kingdom to return to an association of sovereign nations that are part of a common trading market?” Both options were elaborated with detailed notes, with the final wording to be settled by Parliament.

3) When should the referendum be held? Either before, or concurrent with, the next General Election. Urgency was underscored by Chancellor Helmut Kohl’s claim that within two years the creation of a Federal European State would become irreversible—making the next General Election the last chance for British voters to secure a referendum.

4) Aren’t the main parties already offering a referendum? They are, but only on potential entry into a single currency. This is deemed wholly inadequate because it evades the foundational question of sovereignty and the broader constitutional direction of Britain’s relationship with Europe.
